questions.q: For a simple random walk S_n = S_0 + Σ X_i with i.i.d. increments of mean μ and variance σ², what is Var(S_n)?
questions.explain: Since the X_i are independent, variances add: Var(S_n) = n·Var(X_i) = nσ². Variance grows linearly in the number of steps.

questions.q: If the standard deviation of a random walk after n steps is σ√n, how should daily volatility be converted to annual volatility (252 trading days)?
questions.explain: Standard deviation scales with the square root of elapsed time, so annual volatility = daily volatility × √252, not ×252.

questions.q: Why do quants typically model log-prices rather than raw prices as a random walk?
options: Because raw prices can never be random
Because log returns are additive (sums of i.i.d. increments), while raw price changes compound multiplicatively, and sums are far easier to analyze than products
questions.explain: If log-price L_n = L_0 + ΣX_i is a random walk, then price S_n = S_0·exp(ΣX_i) compounds multiplicatively. Additive sums of i.i.d. variables are mathematically far more tractable than products.

questions.q: What does it mean for a random walk to have independent increments?
options: Every step must have a different probability distribution
S_n − S_m (for n > m) depends only on the steps after time m and is independent of the path up to time m
The walk can never return to its starting value
Each step must be exactly +1 or -1
questions.explain: Independent increments mean the change over a future interval doesn't depend on how the walk got to its current position — only on the new i.i.d. steps taken within that interval.

questions.q: A random walk has drift μ = 0 (no expected direction). What is E[S_n] for all n?
options: E[S_n] = S_0, unchanged regardless of n
questions.explain: With zero drift, E[S_n] = S_0 + nμ = S_0 for every n — the expected value never moves away from the starting point, even though the actual path fluctuates randomly.
